WARNING
: Disclosure and circulation
prohibited: The
Code of Civil Procedure
(“C.C.P.”) provides that, except
as authorized by the court, no person shall disclose or circulate any
information that would allow a party or a child whose interests are at stake in
a proceeding in a family matter to be identified (art. 16 C.C.P.).
[1]

1.
INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

This judgement is the result of a seven-day
hearing and the review of some 450 exhibits and an abundance of caselaw.

[
2
]

After a highly-conflictual and outrageously
expensive litigation, Mr. A. E. (the Father) and Mrs. S. G. (the Mother)
seek a divorce.

2.
THE DIVORCE

[
3
]

The parties have lived separate and apart for
nearly four years. There is absolutely no possibility of reconciliation. A
judgement of divorce will be granted.

3.
FAMILY PATRIMONY

[
4
]

The family patrimony and partnership of acquests
was settled by the parties and homologated by the Court on the fifth day of the
hearing. Pursuant to this agreement, the Mother is to receive $275,000.

4.
THE ISSUES

[
5
]

The following issues remain unsettled:

9.1    What is the most appropriate parental plan for their
7-year-old son, X?

9.2    What are the revenues of the Father?

9.3    What is the appropriate quantum of child support for X?

9.4    Is the Mother entitled to spousal support? If so, how much
and for how long?

9.5    Is the Mother entitled for a provision for costs?

9.6    Is the Mother entitled to a lump sum payment?

5.
PARENTAL TIME

5.1  The
context

5.1.1  The
parties

[
6
]

The Father is 43 years old. He has been a member
of the Quebec Bar Association a dozen years. In 2013, he opened a boutique law
firm specializing in commercial litigation. He also invests in real estate and
is interested in collecting cars and trading cards.

[
7
]

The Mother is 39 years old. She is a human
resources specialist. She is currently working as a recruiter (“spécialiste –
acquisition de talents”).
[2]

[
8
]

They met in 2005. They were both students at
University A. The Father was studying political science. She was learning
psychology and subsequently completed a certificate in Human Resources.
Encouraged by her parents, he then studied law and became a member of the Quebec
Bar, articling with her mother, who is a lawyer.

5.1.2  The marriage

[
9
]

After cohabitating a few years, the parties were
married on September 9, 2012, pursuant to the matrimonial regime of Partnership
of Acquests.

[
10
]

X was born on [...], 2015.

5.1.3  The affair

[
11
]

Some three years later, in December 2018, the
Mother discovered that the Father was having an extra marital affair with his
current spouse (Mrs. S.V.).

[
12
]

She was not just any girlfriend. It turns out,
of all things that could befall one, that he was involved with the mother of
three children and the wife of a man accused of various crimes with links with organized
crime.
[3]

[
13
]

The Father admitted that he was worried about
his security. He was being followed and he had received death threats. Security
cameras were installed on the exterior of the family home. He insisted that he
wanted to end this dangerous relationship.

[
14
]

In February 2019, the Mother received a text
message from a certain
“M.”
, that caused concerns:

“Tell your husband to stop fucking
with my friend wife or he might regret it

Yaaaaaa

Tell [him] he is a puece (sic) of
ahit (sic)

He has a family and so does my friend

Tell him to call an eacort (sic)
instead of fucking with my friends wife

He has no idea what he is getting
involved with”
[4]

[
15
]

The threats continued until the Father filed a complaint with the
police in April. This resulted in an Order from the Court for the husband of
Mrs. S.V. not to enter into contact with the Father.

[
16
]

The Mother insisted that the Father stop seeing
Mrs. S.V. to ensure the security of the family. In order to reassure her, he
agreed.

[
17
]

In February, the parties tried to save the
marriage by engaging in couples therapy. This was a failure as their
face-to-face episodes quickly spun out of control. The Father angrily left the
sessions on a number of occasions.

5.1.4  The
separation

[
18
]

There was a lot of arguing and tension. Very
little communication. Hence, in July, the Father left the family residence to take
time to reflect. He moved nearby to his parents’ home.

[
19
]

He continued visiting the family almost every
day after work for an hour or so to spend time with X. He took him, from time
to time, for a few hours on weekends.

[
20
]

In August, he was coming and going. He was
disrupting his son’s bedtime. The Mother did not know where she stood. One day,
she hit the hood of one of his cars with a shovel
[5]
. She was not proud of her loss
of control and for wanting to damage something he prized. She apologized.

[
21
]

With reluctance, in September, the Father agreed
to stay in the family residence for five days to be with X while the Mother was
in Toronto.

[
22
]

He invited Mrs. S.V. to meet him one evening. She
was seen by a neighbour, who informed the Mother.

[
23
]

She was angry. Their relationship was over. She
was not a big fan of Mrs. S.V. and hit back online against her
[6]
. X demand letter was sent to
her to cease such conduct.
[7]

[
24
]

The Mother recalls that it was a period where the
Father was intimidating and aggressive. He constantly wanted to argue with her
in front of X when he came to exercise his access rights. The focus was not on X.
Rather, it was on the legal battle ahead.

[
25
]

She insisted the Father stop coming and going as
he wished. She stood firm that he could see X only on Saturdays from 12h to 17h
and on Sundays from 10h to 17h.

[
26
]

The Father responded by cutting off her access
to the credit card and the bank account. As she was wholly dependent on him, this
caused great distress and left her vulnerable. She had to turn to family and
friends for her basic needs. She took some $3,000 from his account to be able
to survive.

5.1.5  October
14, 2019

[
27
]

On the morning of October 14, things took a
dreadful turn for the worst.

[
28
]

A few days before, the Father entered the family
residence without the Mother’s permission when she was not home. She says she
had enough and could not stand this anymore. She packed his personal belongings
and placed them in the automobile next to X’s car seat.

[
29
]

There are two versions of what occurred that
morning after the Father arrived to pick up X.

[
30
]

The Mother says that, when he got out of his
car, he was “pumped up” and aggressive. He asked for answers on the status of
their negotiations to separate. She hoped he would leave with X and his
personal effects. She needed the keys to the other car. He did not wish to give
them to her, wanting to leave her without the use of a car. He apparently said:

“I am going to put you on the street like the beggar that you are”
and
“you
want war, we are going to war”
in front of X.

[
31
]

The argument lasted some 10 minutes. The Mother
recalls that, at one point, as she moved forward to approach and see X sitting
in the backseat of the car, the Father grabbed her by the collar and shoved her
aside. She nearly fell to the ground.

[
32
]

She phoned the police. As she did so, he got in
the car and left with X.

[
33
]

When the police arrived, they noted that she was
“crying and in distress”. There were no visible injuries.
[8]

[
34
]

The Father has a far different version of events.

[
35
]

He considers that the Mother is unstable and a
liar and denies that he hit her. Nothing happened: he did not touch her. He recalls
that she was “high strung”. She told him she would call the police and tell
them falsely he had assaulted her.

[
36
]

Shortly after, he says that he was at his
parents’ home when the police arrived. He remembers that they “literally…
grabbed” the child out of his arms while they arrested him. He was brought to
the police station. His shoelaces were removed, and he was placed in a holding
cell some four to five hours. He states with emotion, that this was the “most
horrendous” chapter of his life.

[
37
]

He believes that his arrest traumatized X. This likely
caused his behaviour to regress at school.

[
38
]

He points out that, on June 17, 2020, he was
acquitted. Justice St-Onge found that the prosecution did not satisfy their
burden of proof to demonstrate, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the assault
occurred. She found that the Mother had serious credibility issues and that it
was evident that she was hostile towards the Father. She did not believe her
testimony.
[9]

5.1.6  The
legal proceedings

[
39
]

Three days after this series of events, on
October 17, 2019, the Father filed for divorce.

[
40
]

In his application, he said that the false
accusations that led to his arrest show how irresponsible and unstable the
Mother was. He asked for joint custody of the three years old boy to begin
immediately. He stated that the Mother was well-educated but making no attempt
to find employment even though he asked her several times to return to work. He
swore under oath that X was doing very well and integrating nicely in his
kindergarten.

[
41
]

This was the opening to a high-conflict case
that became larger than life. By the time it was heard on its merits, some three
and a half years had passed. The parties came to Court on some 40 to 50
occasions. The disproportionate book of essential procedures, which is
incomplete, has some 100 tabs. The plumitif of procedures of the Superior Court
is 40 pages thick and lists more than 275 entries.

5.2
The
parental plan in place

[
42
]

On November 5, 2019, Justice Carole Hallée,
j.s.c. awarded custody of X to the Mother and granted the Father, as parental
time, two out of three weekends and every Wednesday evening.

[
43
]

On the basis of the revenues declared by the
parties, she ordered the Father to pay the Mother $800 per month in child
support and $2,500 per month in spousal support, once her unemployment
insurance expired. She also ordered him to pay all expenses related to the
family residence and to provide her with the use of a car. Finallly, she
awarded her a provision for costs of $5,000.

5.3
Post-separation
troubles begin

[
44
]

A month later, the Mother complained to the
Court that the Father was complicating matters. Despite the fact that he is
himself a lawyer, he hired two lawyers from different law firms. This was making procedures cumbersome and expensive:
“le nombre
de correspondances reçues de ses avocats est démesuré eut égard aux questions
en litige me faisant encourir des frais importants”
.
[10]

5.4
The child

[
45
]

Having established the above context, let’s now
turn our attention to what is in the best interest of X.

[
46
]

The pictures submitted in evidence reveal that he
is a good-looking young boy.

[
47
]

The parents describe him as a “great kid”,
affectionate, loving, sweet, inquisitive and very intelligent. He reads two to
three books a day and gets great marks in mathematics. He loves music, soccer
and basketball, taking walks and playing videogames. He has a very good sense
of humour.

[
48
]

Despite those strengths, he has serious challenges
in social interactions.

[
49
]

The parents recognize that, since the age of
two, he presents significant behavioral and emotional difficulties: he readily
bites, scratches, pushes, hits and screams. He is quick to anger and struggles
controlling his emotions. He can be impatient and aggressive. He has trouble
following instructions at home and at school. He has problems transitioning
from one activity to another. He is also reported to have displayed several
tics and to have challenges sleeping.

[
50
]

He was diagnosed, in August 2020, with severe
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) as well as Oppositional
Defiance Disorder (ODD). He also suffers from anxiety.

[
51
]

These issues have been present and a constant
struggle since he began daycare. By the time he started kindergarten, he had to
change daycare four times. He needs a full-time, integration aide, or shadow,
who can step in when he becomes aggressive
[11]
.
Because of this, he was not able to attend daycare or kindergarten full-time.

[
52
]

X is currently in grade 2 at School A.

[
53
]

The most recent assessments of September and
October, 2022 by an occupational therapist
[12]

confirm that he continues to need a full-time shadow with him at school. They
indicate that he has difficulty understanding his emotions and making
appropriate decisions when faced with big feelings. When frustrated, he can
lose control and act inappropriately. It is recommended that he continue to get
help with his behavioral therapist to regulate his emotions.

[
54
]

X is currently medicated. He receives by-weekly
behavioral therapy and bi-weekly occupational therapy. The most recent report
indicates that he is making progress, but he needs ongoing support to deal with
his emotions and his anxiety:

X has been receiving behavioral services at our clinic
since November 2020. He has made several gains and has matured quite a bit
since then. However, X gets older ongoing support to help with his behavioral
needs, namely emotional regulation, making and maintaining social
relationships, as well as managing anxiety will be important. For example, at
school there will be instances where X will become physically or verbally
aggressive with a peer when he becomes upset or is unhappy with a situation. As
well, if an adult tells him to do something that he does not want to do in the
moment he can refuse to do the task or completely shut down and ignore the
adult. There have however been some marked improvements in these occurrences.
[13]

His homeroom teacher reported, on February 15, 2023,
that a behavior technician is assigned to X and works with him every day. He is
doing well academically but he “can sometimes have anger and behavioral issues
that make it hard for him to be engaged in class and connect with his peers”.
[14]

[
55
]

X’s daycare technician of the after-school
program reports that there has been “no major behaviour incidents” this school year
.
[15]

5.5
The
position of the parties

5.5.1
The
Father

[
56
]

The Father proclaims his desire to be an active
parent. He is asking for joint 50/50 parental time. He wants to spend every
other week with X. He says that he is a loving father and that X tells him he
misses him. He would like to be more involved. Currently, he feels left out.

[
57
]

He explains that he owns a cottage and rents a
three-bedroom apartment that he shares with Mrs. S.V. and her twelve-year-old
daughter (in shared parental time) and their small dog, Chewy. X has his own
bedroom.

[
58
]

He points out that the psychosocial expertise of
August 2021 recommended a shared parenting time starting in January 2022. That
was over a year ago.

[
59
]

He is convinced that the child was weaponized in
this protracted legal battle. He points out how inflexible the Mother is. Since
the beginning, she has not moved an inch in his direction. Rather, she is
proposing less access rights that he currently has.

5.5.2
The Mother

[
60
]

The Mother contests the Father’s proposed shared
parental plan for several reasons.

[
61
]

To begin, she has serious reservations with the
psychosocial expertise.

[
62
]

Further, given X’s behavioral issues, she
provides him greater stability and availability.

[
63
]

As well, she says that the Father is aggressive
and conflictual. He is unable to communicate with her respectfully. He does not
collaborate or support her. She is convinced that he is not focused on X’s
needs.

[
64
]

Finally, she points out that his actions and
words are not aligned as he has not been consistent with his access rights in
the past.

[
65
]

She, therefore, proposes that the Father have parental
time with X one weekend out of two from Saturday 10:00am to Monday at school to
be followed by pedagogical days. She agrees that, if all goes well, and X does
not regress, she is open to enlarging those access rights from Friday after
school to Monday morning at school.

5.6
The
law

[
66
]

The
Divorce Act
stipulates that, when a
Court makes a decision concerning parental time, it shall “take into
consideration only the best interest of the child”
[16]
. It is to give primary
considerations to the child’s physical, emotional and psychological safety,
security and well-being
[17]
.

[
67
]

In order to determine the best interest of a
child, the
Divorce Act
enumerates a list of non-exhaustive factors to
consider:

(a)

the
child’s needs, given the child’s age and stage of development, such as the
child’s need for stability;

(b)

the
nature and strength of the child’s relationship with each spouse, each of the
child’s siblings and grandparents and any other person who plays an important
role in the child’s life;

(c)

each
spouse’s willingness to support the development and maintenance of the child’s
relationship with other spouse;

(d)

the
history of care of the child;

(e)

the
child’s views and preferences, giving due weight of the child’s age and
maturity, unless they cannot be ascertained;

(f)

the
child’s cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage,
including Indigenous upbringing and heritage;

(g)

any
plans for the child’s care;

(h)

the
ability and willingness of each person in respect of whom the order would apply
to care for and meet the needs of the child;

(i)

the
ability and willingness of each person in respect of whom the order would apply
to communicate and cooperate, in particular with one another, on matters
affecting the child;

(j)

any
family violence and its impact on, among other things,

(i)

the
ability and willingness of any person who engaged in the family violence to
care for and meet the needs of the child, and

(ii)

the appropriateness of
making an order that would require persons in respect of whom the order would
apply to cooperate on issues affecting the child; and

(k)

any
civil or criminal proceeding, order, condition, or measure that is relevant to
the safety, security and well-being of the child.
[18]

[
68
]

In a similar fashion,
article 33
of the
Civil Code of Quebec

(the
CCQ) stipulates that every decision concerning a child shall be taken in light
of his best interest.

[
69
]

To determine whether shared parenting time is
the appropriate solution, the following factors are generally considered:

•

the parental capacities of each parent;

•

the availability of each parent;

•

the proximity of the residence of the parents;

•

the stability of the child;

•

the educational values of the parents and their
parental skills;

•

the ability to communicate adequately and the
absence of conflict;

•

the desire expressed by the child if he/she has
the maturity to express it.

[
70
]

None of these factors are determinative. They
need to be analyzed globally.

5.7
The psychosocial
expertise

[
71
]

Before we consider and apply the abovementioned
criteria to the case at hand, let’s look at what the Court appointed expert
discovered and concluded.
[19]

[
72
]

In July and August 2021, Mr. Wim De Wit,
L.Ps., had Zoom meetings and individual interviews in his office with both the
Father and the Mother. He also met individually with the Father, the Mother and
X to assess their interactions. He reviewed the reports from X’s psychologist
and consulted the behavioral consultant. He spoke as well with Mrs. S.V.

[
73
]

He administered two objective personality
evaluations to each of the parents.

[
74
]

With respect to the parental capacity of the
Mother, he states as follows:

•

The
Mother, (…), is an attentive mother, who is able to respond in an adequate way
to X’s different needs. She has a certain ease in detecting the challenges of
her son and in the way she speaks about X, we feel that she deploys an
attentive and observational approach. She has offered X both the general
structure and routine that he needs as well as having occupied a central place
in the implementation of the general stability in his life and she knows her
son very well.

•

The
Mother is a present and available mother, who is clearly invested in her role
and who wants to assure the development of her son and offer a constructive
upbringing. She actively expresses her affection towards X. She wants to teach X
that everybody has a different perspective and that it is important to respect
their opinion.

[
75
]

Concerning the Father’s parental capacities, Mr.
De Wit is more nuanced. He writes:

The Father gravitated towards a new relationship at
the end of his relationship with the Mother, without necessarily respecting X’s
rhythm in the introduction of a new partner, although we understood that the
couple took their time before living together and respected a progressive
integration.

[
76
]

He found that he lacked insight and did not
always act in the child’s best interest:

He is a father who loves his son and who expresses his
affection. He had a more fluctuating availability in the past, as he was in the
role of provider and breadwinner. More recently, he decided to suspend his
contact avec X, which we do not believe to be in the child’s interest. Even if
the Father desperately wants a more convenient parenting situation, his current
lack of presence can have a negative impact on his attachment bond with X and
create feelings of confusion, insecurity and abandonment for his son. He wants
to offer a positive environment to his son and assure he can be happy and
autonomous/independent. He recognizes the parental capacities of the Mother,
but he feels easily attacked by her comments and statements. He seems to
attribute the main responsibility for their difficult co-parenting to the
Mother; lacking a degree of insight or appropriate tools on his own part and
refusing his part of responsibility in the creation of the current dysfunctional
atmosphere.

[
77
]

Having administered the personality tests, Mr. De
Wit concluded as follows about the Mother:

The Mother does not present any clear signs of
pathology on a psychological level, even if certain areas can be a little more
fragile. She is practical and conventional in her approach to life; she is also
responsible and conforming. She is generally optimistic and positive in her
outlook on life. She has a certain tendency to please others and might deny
conflict. She can also develop some physical symptoms when stress and
resentment build and she can have areas in her life where she represses
negative emotions. She can take setbacks badly and blame herself on those occasions.

We observe the presence of a high amount of socially
acceptable answers and she tried to present herself as a person who is morally
virtuous and emotionally under control. It is possible that certain problems in
her functioning are not detected because of this and that the validity of the
results is lowered. We observe that she does not present any major issues in
her functioning, which corroborates the results of the first test. We observe
here also evidence that she might react with physical symptoms to external
stressors and she mentions the presence of fatigue and difficulty to sleep and
a lack of energy.

[
78
]

8.1
The
position of the parties

8.2
The
law

[
205
]

Section 15.2
of the
Divorce Act

sets out
the framework for the sometimes difficult and complex analysis required in
examining the issue of spousal support.

[
206
]

The following provisions are pertinent. They set
out the factors and objectives to be taken into consideration:

15.2
(1)  A court of
competent jurisdiction may, on application by either or both spouses, make an
order requiring a spouse to secure or pay, or to secure and pay, such lump sum
or periodic sums, or such lump sum and periodic sums, as the court thinks
reasonable for the support of the other spouse.
[…]

(4) In making an order under
subsection (1) or an interim order under subsection (2) the court shall take
into consideration the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each
spouse, including

(a) the length of time the spouses
cohabited;

(b) the functions performed by each
spouse during cohabitation; and

(c) any order, agreement or
arrangement relating to support of either spouse.
[…]

(6) An order made under subsection
(1) or an interim order under subsection (2) that provides for the support of a
spouse should

(a) recognize any economic advantages
or disadvantages to the spouses arising from the marriage or its breakdown;

(b) apportion between the spouses any
financial consequences arising from the care of any child of the marriage over
and above any obligation for the support of any child of the marriage;

(c) relieve any economic hardship of
the spouses arising from the breakdown of the marriage; and

(d) in so far as practicable, promote
the economic self-sufficiency of each spouse within a reasonable period of
time.

[
207
]

The purpose of spousal support is to relieve the economic hardship
that results from the marriage and its breakdown. All four objectives of
Section 15(6) are to be taken into account. None are paramount or to be given
priority. A broad approach is required.

8.3
Analysis

[
208
]

The first objective of
Section 15(6)
of the
Divorce
Act
requires the Court to consider the economic advantages and
disadvantages arising from the marriage and its breakdown. It permits the Court
to compensate one party for the sacrifices made during the marriage and for the
benefits which the other one received.

[
209
]

The second aim to be taken into consideration is
the
“apportionment”
of the financial consequences of raising the
children. If one of the party continues to suffer a financial disadvantage
because of this, he or she must be compensated.

[
210
]

The third purpose to be examined is whether
economic hardship has been created by the breakdown of the marriage.

[
211
]

The final goal to be considered is
“when
practical”
to promote the economic self-sufficiency.

advantages and disadvantages

[

Court has discretion in such matters:

"
Elle dépend des circonstances en l’espèce et
le Tribunal a discrétion en cette matière. Il ne doit pas être accordée pour
encourager et alimenter des procédures abusives et des débats futiles mais elle

10.2
The
law

[
359
]

Article 15.2(1)
of the
Divorce Act

states:

15.2
(1)  A court of competent
jurisdiction may, on application by either or both spouses, make an order
requiring a spouse to secure or pay, or to secure and pay, such lump sum or periodic
sums, or such lump sum and periodic sums, as the court thinks reasonable for
the support of the other spouse.

[
360
]

A lump sum is alimentary in nature. It is attributed according to
the means and the needs of the parties while taking into account the advantages
and inconveniences that stem from the marriage. The Court of Appeal has often
analyzed the required criteria to succeed in such a claim.

[
361
]

In
Droit
de la famille – 121300
[74]
,
it stated :

[27]  La somme globale est de nature
alimentaire ce qui entraîne qu’elle doit être attribuée selon les moyens du
débiteur et les besoins du créancier. Les raisons qui justifient d’accorder une
somme globale sont multiples. La Cour a formulé une énumération non exhaustive
dans l’arrêt Droit de la famille – 2091. Entre autres, la somme globale peut
servir à couvrir les frais pour se reloger, le paiement des honoraires des
avocats, ou encore, à assurer la sécurité financière future du créancier
alimentaire.

10.3
Analysis and Decision

[
362
]

The Court considers that the Mother presents a
valid claim for a lump sum.

[
363

Having however taken into consideration the sum
received by her following the partition of the family patrimony, the payment of
child and spousal support and the provision for costs, the Court considers that
a lump sum payment is not possible.

[
364
]

The Court is unconvinced that the Father has assets
and revenues sufficient to pay a sum that would help the Mother. Even though,
his true financial situation is still murky, there is no evidence that he has
the means to pay any further sum.
